lesson.title: Proteins on Duty: The Working Parts of the Plasma Membrane
lesson.summary: Beyond its lipid barrier, the plasma membrane is packed with proteins that transport molecules, relay signals, and identify the cell to its neighbors, turning a simple lipid boundary into an active, communicating surface.
lesson.body:
A phospholipid bilayer alone would make an effective barrier, but a cell needs far more than a barrier. It needs to import specific nutrients, export specific waste, sense signals from outside, and recognize other cells. Nearly all of that functionality comes from membrane proteins, the protein component covered generally in the chapter on proteins, now embedded within or attached to the plasma membrane described earlier in this course.

Membrane proteins fall into two broad categories based on how they associate with the bilayer. Integral proteins are embedded within the membrane itself, and many are transmembrane proteins that span the entire bilayer, often crossing back and forth several times as a folded chain of alpha helices, with hydrophobic amino acid stretches sitting comfortably in the membrane's hydrophobic interior and hydrophilic stretches exposed to water on either side. Peripheral proteins, by contrast, do not enter the bilayer at all; they attach loosely to the membrane surface, often by binding to the exposed parts of integral proteins or to the hydrophilic phospholipid heads.

These proteins carry out several distinct jobs. Transport proteins, either channels that form a pore for specific molecules or carriers that bind and shuttle a molecule across, move substances that cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer on their own, a function explored further in the chapters on selective permeability and passive transport. Receptor proteins bind signaling molecules arriving from outside the cell and trigger a response inside, the starting point of most cell signaling pathways. Some membrane proteins act as enzymes, catalyzing reactions right at the membrane surface, while others serve as anchors for cell adhesion, physically linking a cell to its neighbors or to a supporting structural matrix.

A further class of membrane proteins, often studded with attached carbohydrate chains and then called glycoproteins, functions as an identification tag. These carbohydrate markers on the outer surface of the plasma membrane let a cell display an identity that other cells and the immune system can read. The human ABO blood type system is a concrete example: red blood cells carry glycoproteins and glycolipids with slightly different attached sugar structures depending on blood type, and the immune system uses those differences to distinguish self from incompatible blood.

A real transport example worth knowing is the glucose transporter family, called GLUT proteins, integral membrane proteins that bind glucose on one side of the membrane and release it on the other, allowing this essential but polar sugar to move into cells that cannot let it pass directly through the hydrophobic bilayer. Together with the phospholipid bilayer covered in earlier chapters, this diverse set of proteins is what the fluid mosaic model describes as the scattered, varied tiles of the membrane's mosaic, and it is what turns a simple lipid barrier into a fully functional, communicating cell surface.
